name: Dichanthium
look_here_first: KLEBERG and SILKY are both introduced Dichanthium. BOTH may have a broad white hair beard at true stem nodes; neither the ring nor purple silvery heads alone separates them. Walk from rooted plant to complete clustered head, check raceme stalks and basal sterile pairs, then measure mature spikelet glume margins and awns. KR has similarly terminal slender fingers and may have short hairy nodes; inspect upper leaf-blade papilla hairs and fertile glumes.

recognition.where_to_look_first: KLEBERG and SILKY are both introduced Dichanthium. BOTH may have a broad white hair beard at true stem nodes; neither the ring nor purple silvery heads alone separates them. Walk from rooted plant to complete clustered head, check raceme stalks and basal sterile pairs, then measure mature spikelet glume margins and awns. KR has similarly terminal slender fingers and may have short hairy nodes; inspect upper leaf-blade papilla hairs and fertile glumes.
priority: 1. Photograph entire rooted plant and all terminal raceme branch origins, not a detached head.
2. Photograph true stem node hair ring with mm scale, then compare Kleberg, Silky and native cane; node ring is not unique.
3. Check Kleberg's often pedunculate/subdigitate racemes versus more sessile densely villous Silky head; count is not decisive.
4. In mature attached spikelet pairs, inspect lower glume broad shape, upper marginal hairs and reduced pedicelled companion.
5. Against KR, check upper blade stiff papilla hairs and nodal short-versus-long hair pattern (both variable); preserve unknown ID if not enough.

comparison_lesson.title: Dichanthium two-species field comparison
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: KLEBERG and SILKY can BOTH have white BEARDED NODES. KLEBERG often stalked subdigitate head, SILKY often densely silky and more sessile; KR also has grouped fingers. Confirm MATURE SPIKELETS.
quick_split: D. annulatum Kleberg (introduced): often 2–15 slender clustered racemes; spreading white nodal beard in many plants; some stoloniferous bases. Basal spikelet pairs may be sterile, mature glume often broadly obtuse with upper ciliate margins.

D. sericeum silky (introduced in Texas, native Australia): densely hairy usually 2–6 closely grouped racemes and similarly white-bearded true nodes. Glumes often show characteristic long subapical hair fringe.

B. ischaemum King Ranch (introduced): several LONG slender racemes converge at tip, often stiff papilla-based hairs above blade collar; short node hairs VARIABLE. Flowering silhouette alone cannot separate from Kleberg.
Native cane B. barbinodis can also have strongly bearded true nodes; rule out via broad fanlike head and matched spikelets.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: A conspicuous nodal WHITE RING is shared and overlaps native cane; no species-level or invasive native/introduced decision should rest on the hair ring alone. FNA North American D. annulatum nodes may be smooth or short-pubescent. In Texas both canonical Dichanthium taxa are introduced; protect other native bluestems while the ID remains unresolved.

comparison_matrix.title: Dichanthium practical species-key comparisons
rows: Frequently conspicuous long spreading white ring; FNA North America describes sometimes smooth or SHORT-haired too.
Prominent spreading white ring also documented in licensed exact-species Australian photos; shared trait, NOT the key.
Commonly stalked, subdigitate 2–9 or more racemes; lowest spikelet pairs commonly awnless/male/sterile.
Densely white-villous racemes often subsessile or sessile; raceme count variable, overlapping Kleberg.
Can have rooted/prostrate basal stolons and ascending culms; not unique to Kleberg.
Often more tightly tufted; individual plants may overlap, so keep second trait.
Sessile lower glume often broadly obtuse, 2–3 teeth; long marginal cilia near tip and twisted bent awn. Mate with sterile pedicelled spikelet.
Sessile lower glume with transverse subapical hair fringe; both have awned fertile sessile and sterile pedicelled partner. Macro with attached axis needed.
Archived Macleay flowerhead + new licensed node, full head and single awned spikelet; no matched Texas voucher.
One archived licensed noncommercial inflorescence plus two licensed Commons node and full tuft views; no measured glume macros.

field_traits: Often sprawling or creeping via stolonlike lower shoots and eventually ascending erect to about 1 m.
A prominent node collar of WHITE HAIRS is a signature feature; must be photographed at node, not assumed from panicle.
Inflorescence of 2–15 fingerlike racemes bearing paired sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets.
Spikelets often silvery or purplish, with hairy axes and awned fertile florets; numbers vary.
Introduced/invasive management grass, NOT native restoration seed.
comparisons.how_to_split: D. sericeum is an introduced silky bluestem also with very hairy silvery flowering branches, but often tufted with shorter rhizomes rather than distinctly stoloniferous. D. annulatum is strongly associated with unmistakable white-ringed stem nodes, and its full flowering head may bear more subdigitate racemes. Distinguish both from Bothriochloa/Schizachyrium with paired-spikelet + glume macro; photo of a red-purple foxtail alone is insufficient.

field_traits: Often tufted perennial to about 1 m, sometimes with short rhizomes; annual/perennial treatments may differ by subspecies.
Culms can have hairy or bearded nodes and narrow linear-lanceolate leaf blades.
Many silky long hairs around spikelet pairs and axes yield pale, sometimes purple, fuzzy appearance.
Sessile fertile spikelet around 4 mm in Flora Zambesiaca treatment; awn twisted, bent, sometimes ~25 mm.
Texas occurrence introduced according to Kew; do not place into local-native dashboard metrics.
comparisons.how_to_split: Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) usually has more clearly 2–15 fingerlike racemes and prominently WHITE-RINGED stem nodes, sometimes a creeping/stoloniferous base. D. sericeum's densely silky hair and narrow racemes are useful orientation cues, NOT decisive alone; mature spikelet, paired sterile companion, node and root base necessary. Both species introduced in Texas.

what_to_teach_crew: First confirm true stem NODE versus leaf COLLAR and capture both; node hairs are shared with Kleberg, Silky, and potentially native cane.
Compare the photographed complete head to KR's converging long fingers; all may resemble one another.
True mature paired spikelet macro and lower-glume apex are required when the head architecture overlaps.
Distinguish native versus introduced carefully: management decisions may group invasive KR and Kleberg, but avoid removing native bluestems on a hairy node alone.
Photos are nonlocal licensed anatomical demonstrations; do not imply local Hays presence, nativity or proof of local morphotypes.
visual_needs: Paired local Kleberg versus KR upper blade papilla and TRUE node hair macro with 1 mm ruler
Matched full Kleberg/Silky/King Ranch flowering heads and true basal branch insertion
Mature attached paired spikelets and fertile lower-glume margins on Kleberg/Silky and KR
Actual local source-vouchered whole rooted grass, including basal stolons and sheath ligule
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 2/2 canonical Dichanthium species expanded with photos of true node ring, reproductive head and whole plant; Texas attached macro and species-pair glume comparison still missing.

visual_comparison.title: Dichanthium and KR — source-photographed stem nodes, flowerheads, awns and tuft
visual_comparison.subtitle: Two Dichanthium existing physically archived photos plus FIVE new exact-species, individually licensed external views. One Texas KR comparison with live provenance. No diagnostic glume hairs are arrowed without actual resolving pixels.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: KLEBERG and SILKY can BOTH have white BEARDED NODES. KLEBERG often stalked subdigitate head, SILKY often densely silky and more sessile; KR also has grouped fingers. Confirm MATURE SPIKELETS.

items.label: Kleberg node
items.image_role: Actual true culm node ringed with LONG WHITE HAIRS; Australian Kleberg bluestem; NOT a lone species-level proof
items.caption: Inspect the actual STEM NODE (not the collar where leaf blade meets sheath). This is a genuine dense white halo. Texas KR plants sometimes have SHORT node hairs, and silky bluestem also has a bearded node, so follow up with full head and spikelets.
items.why_it_matters: Key identification structure on a real stem, not the leaf collar; shared hair trait with Silky; evaluate in combination.
items.creator: Harry Rose / Macleay Grass Man
items.photo_status: Wikimedia Commons Flickr-verified CC BY 2.0; photo viewed 2026-10-21 and gross-structure arrow positions based on displayed 960px image; original photograph from Summer Island, New South Wales, Australia; external Commons reference, NOT physically archived.

items.label: Kleberg head
items.image_role: Full subdigitate terminal inflorescence showing 4–5 slender spikelet-bearing racemes and lower convergence point
items.caption: Follow several erect stalked reproductive racemes down to their junction. The basal spikelet pairs may be sterile/unawned; individual fertile versus sterile florets require a magnifier. This silhouette resembles KR: 3–8 fingers alone are NOT a safe distinction.
items.why_it_matters: Shows the entire raceme branch topology against KR, which may be superficially identical.
items.creator: Harry Rose / Macleay Grass Man
items.photo_status: Wikimedia Commons Flickr-verified CC BY 2.0; photo viewed 2026-10-21 and gross-structure arrow positions based on displayed 960px image; original photograph from Summer Island, New South Wales, Australia; external Commons reference, NOT physically archived.

items.label: Kleberg spikelet
items.image_role: Isolated awned sessile fertile spikelet, complete long bent awn and glume silhouette against contrasting gray background
items.caption: This one mature awned spikelet allows the crew to trace the long bent awn back to its grass glumes. Its sterile PEDICELLED PARTNER is NOT in this photograph, and individual lower-glume edge hairs cannot be measured from this view.
items.why_it_matters: Shows awn/glume anatomy on ONE mature spikelet. Missing its pedicelled companion prevents definitive species call alone.
items.creator: Harry Rose / Macleay Grass Man
items.photo_status: Wikimedia Commons Flickr-verified CC BY 2.0; photo viewed 2026-10-21 and gross-structure arrow positions based on displayed 960px image; original photograph from Summer Island, New South Wales, Australia; external Commons reference, NOT physically archived.

items.label: Silky node
items.image_role: Dichanthium sericeum true vegetative stem node with substantial white spreading hair ring
items.caption: SILKY BLUESTEM also grows a fluffy white node beard. This disproves the simplistic 'white hairy ring = only Kleberg' rule. Compare attached flowering head and microscopically measured glumes for species-level certainty.
items.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the important node-ring OVERLAP: a white hairy node cannot alone separate the two Dichanthium species.
items.creator: Harry Rose / Macleay Grass Man
items.photo_status: Wikimedia Commons Flickr-verified CC BY 2.0; photo viewed 2026-10-21 and gross-structure arrow positions based on displayed 960px image; original photograph from Dungog, New South Wales, Australia; external Commons reference, NOT physically archived.

items.label: Silky habit
items.image_role: Whole flowering tuft of source-identified silky bluestem in its native Australian habitat
items.caption: See the relatively tight tuft carrying narrow hairy terminal raceme clusters. The view does NOT show species-level glume characters or hidden roots; growing context is Australian and should not imply this plant is native to Texas.
items.why_it_matters: Adds whole-plant flowering architecture while keeping nonlocal source explicit.
items.creator: Harry Rose / Macleay Grass Man
items.photo_status: Wikimedia Commons Flickr-verified CC BY 2.0; photo viewed 2026-10-21 and gross-structure arrow positions based on displayed 960px image; original photograph from New South Wales, Australia; external Commons reference, NOT physically archived.

items.label: Texas KR bluestem — compare terminal fingers
items.image_role: Texas field view of terminal panicle: many long narrow branches, CC BY photograph
items.caption: Austin-area source-labelled var. songarica flowering stem with numerous branches clustered near the terminal axis. Visible terminal panicle architecture is useful; no true plant base, leaf collar or individual glume anatomy is legible in this photograph.
items.why_it_matters: KR has several long terminal racemes TOO. Contrast with a confirmed Kleberg hairy node + attached spikelet details; do not identify by fingers alone.
items.creator: Tyler Cannon
items.photo_status: Visually inspected 960px Commons reference on 2026-10-21. Exact Texas source concept and CC BY 4.0 verified; external source, no downloaded local image bytes.

items.label: Kleberg bluestem — inspected source photograph
items.image_role: Original local physically stored source-identified photo, inspected on 2026-10-21 for gross structures
items.caption: Original photo visibly shows an erect bundle of slender pigmented seed-bearing branches and long fine awns. It cannot resolve the diagnostic WHITE RING at the vegetative stem node, which lies off-frame.
items.why_it_matters: Introduced invasive warm-season Kleberg bluestem. Start at the 2–15 thin upright/fingerlike paired-spikelet racemes and examine a RING of conspicuous WHITE HAIRS at stem nodes, which is especially useful in this species. Magnify sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets, the awn and lower glume; a hairy pinkish head alone is not species proof.
items.creator: Macleay Grass Man (Harry Rose)
items.photo_status: Original in-repo photo and rights preserved. Gross visible structural arrows only; no pixel verification of ligules, microscopic lemma details or roots; original source determination not independently specimen-confirmed.

items.label: Silky bluestem — inspected source photograph
items.image_role: Original local physically stored source-identified photo, inspected on 2026-10-21 for gross structures
items.caption: Source photograph shows a small narrow silver hairy flowering axis held before grassland; the photograph does NOT show legible spikelet glume hairs, true collar, or roots.
items.why_it_matters: Introduced SILKY BLUESTEM (not a native Texas bluestem). Examine the silvery-hairy flowering head and narrow, often paired racemes, and then magnify the companion sterile/pedicelled spikelet against the awned sessile fertile spikelet. Compare the basal clump and hairy stem nodes against invasive Kleberg bluestem. This photo shows only one small silky head held against fingers, not definitive spikelet dissection.
items.creator: Melissa Walsh
items.photo_status: Original in-repo photo and rights preserved. Gross visible structural arrows only; no pixel verification of ligules, microscopic lemma details or roots; original source determination not independently specimen-confirmed.
